(5) Legislative Rules Excepted from Notice and Comment for 
‘‘Good Cause^^
APA section 553(b)(B) says that notice and comment is not required 
“when the agency for good cause finds (and incorporates the finding and a 
brief statement of reasons therefor in the rules issued) that notice and 
public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the 
public interest.” Note that the agency must invoke this exception at the 
time it promulgates the rule; doing so in litigation afterward is too late. 
Whether the agency was correct to find “good cause” is a question subject 
to judicial review. Some circuits engage in de novo review of whether the 
agency had “good cause” to forego notice and comment, e.g., Sorenson 
Communications Inc. v. FCC, 755 F.3d 702, 706 (D.C. Cir. 2014), while 
others have used the arbitrary-or-capricious standard for this 
determination, e.g.. United States v. Johnson, 632 F.3d 912, 928 (5th Cir. 
2011).
According to a study by the Government Accountability Office, the 
good cause exception is invoked fi’equently. U.S. GOV’T ACCOUNTABILITY

sample into “major” and “nonmajor” rules, according to the definition of 
“major” in the Congressional Review Act (i.e., having a likely annual effect 
on the economy of $100 million or more). GAO found that 35 percent of 
major rules and 44 percent of nonmajor rules were promulgated without a 
prior notice of proposed rulemaking. For the notice-less rules in the sample, 
good cause was the most commonly invoked exception by far: it accounted 
for 77 percent of the notice-less major rules and 61 percent of the notice-
less nonmajor rules.^o GAO added:
